book.title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
book.author: Stephen R. Covey

confidence_note: Covey tells this first-person anecdote in the 'Paradigms and Principles' part of the book to illustrate a paradigm shift. Retold in our own words; no long quotation from the book.
facts: A Sunday morning on a New York subway car; passengers calm — reading newspapers, lost in thought, resting with eyes closed.
A man boards with his children; the children immediately get loud and rowdy, throwing things, even grabbing people's papers; the whole car is disturbed.
The man sits next to Covey with his eyes closed, apparently oblivious.
Covey is irritated and can't believe the man lets his children run wild and takes no responsibility.
With what he considered unusual patience and restraint, Covey asks the man whether he could control his children a little more because they are disturbing people.

The man looks up as if just becoming aware, and says softly that Covey is right, that he guesses he should do something; they have just come from the hospital where the children's mother died about an hour ago; he doesn't know what to think, and he guesses the children don't know how to handle it either.

Covey: in that instant he saw things differently, and because he saw differently he thought, felt and behaved differently; his irritation vanished; he didn't have to control his attitude — his heart filled with the man's pain; he asked about it and how he could help.
The children's behaviour had not changed; Covey's paradigm had.
tension: The reader should first feel Covey's irritation, then have their own judgment overturned.
opening_idea: Ask the listener to picture someone who annoyed them this week.

lessons.idea: We react to the lens, not the behaviour: Covey didn't force himself calm; his view changed and feelings and behaviour followed.
lessons.anchor: children still loud, Covey's reaction transformed

lessons.idea: Everyone in the car wrote the same story and no one asked; one question revealed the truth.
lessons.anchor: the whole car judging the 'careless father'

lessons.idea: This is not a 'never say anything' story: Covey was right that the kids were disruptive; the point is to hold judgment loosely and leave room for the other person's story. Not every situation hides a tragedy.
lessons.anchor: Covey's polite request is what opened the truth

reflect: What story did you write in your head about the person you pictured?
How much of that story do you actually know, and how much is a guess?
Have you asked them if everything is okay?
Have you ever been the father on the train — judged on a bad day by people who didn't know?
reflect_final: being the father on the train

use_cases.situation: meeting, a teammate keeps missing deadlines and the room turns to blame
use_cases.move: tell the subway story briefly and suggest talking first

use_cases.situation: manager's one-on-one with someone whose performance dropped
use_cases.move: open with a question instead of a verdict

use_cases.situation: an angry customer email or tense message
use_cases.move: before replying, ask what's happening in their 'train car'

use_cases.situation: at home, a partner or child snaps unexpectedly
use_cases.move: ask 'did something happen today?' instead of 'why are you talking like that?'
am I reacting to what they did, or to the story I wrote?

pocket_idea: The children didn't change; Covey's lens did. Ask before you judge.
